whyCorrect: The first two sentences describe failure in both directions: too light and the bell does not sound properly, too heavy and the metal is damaged. A blank that has to satisfy both limits at once is asking for correspondence between clapper and casting, so the weight has to be matched to the casting. The phrase "within narrow limits" confirms it: there is a right size, and only a small range of it.

whyWrong.B: Opposed reverses the logic. Nothing in the text suggests the clapper should work against the casting; both failures come from the weight not suiting the bell.
whyWrong.C: Secondary would say the clapper matters less than the casting, but the text spends both examples showing that clapper weight decides whether the bell sounds or cracks.
whyWrong.D: Invisible describes appearance, not weight, and a clapper hanging inside a bell is out of sight regardless of how heavy it is.

commonMistakes: Reading only the second sentence and concluding the point is about damage, rather than noticing that the first sentence describes the opposite error.
tips: When a text gives you a failure at each extreme, the blank almost always names the middle condition that avoids both.

whyCorrect: The text sets up a contrast: a line brought properly up to heat fuses and cannot be rubbed off, while a line the furnace left short of that heat behaves differently. The blank names what an unfused line is, and the clue is that it will be gone within a century of weather. Paint that never joined the surface is only sitting on top of it, so it is resting on the glass.

whyWrong.A: Fused to the glass is exactly what the underheated line is not. The sentence before it reserves fusing for a line brought properly up to heat.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the passage involves cutting or engraving. The paint is brushed on and heated, not incised.
whyWrong.C: Hidden under the glass contradicts the description of the paint as a layer laid on the surface with a brush, and being hidden would not explain why weather removes it.

commonMistakes: Choosing fused because the word appears twice in the passage; the blank describes the failed line, not the successful one.

whyCorrect: The rule stated first is that no bell may move more than one place between rows. The second sentence spells out the consequence: a band reaches a new arrangement only through a chain of rows each differing slightly from the last. A change built up in small stages is incremental.

whyWrong.A: Instantaneous is the opposite of what the rule produces. The text says a band cannot jump straight to an arrangement it fancies.
whyWrong.C: Arbitrary would mean the order changes without constraint, but the whole passage is about a constraint that governs every row.
whyWrong.D: Inaudible has nothing to do with the ordering rule, and bells being rung are plainly meant to be heard.

tips: The blank is completing the consequence of a rule already stated, so restate the rule in your own words before you look at the choices.

whyCorrect: The carillonneur hears the bells from a few metres away through the louvres, not from the square where listeners are. The next sentence reports that street-level recordings regularly surprise players, which means their sense of balance does not match what the audience actually hears. A judgement that regularly turns out to be wrong is unreliable.

whyWrong.A: Unrehearsed refers to preparation. The problem is where the player is sitting, not how much practice has gone in.
whyWrong.C: Unnecessary would mean the player need not judge balance at all, but balance is precisely what the player is trying to control.
whyWrong.D: Unmistakable says the judgement is clear and certain, which contradicts the recordings that surprise them.

commonMistakes: Reading "surprise" as a neutral word; here it signals that the player's expectation was wrong.

whyCorrect: The final sentence describes something inherited that is narrow enough to exclude other species yet loose enough to be filled in by local song. That is a pattern with slots left open, which is what a template is. The evidence supports it: raised in silence the bird cannot produce a real song, so it does not inherit the song itself, but it still rejects another species' song, so it inherits some constraint on what counts.

whyWrong.A: A rehearsal is an act of practising, not something that can be inherited or filled in.
whyWrong.C: A repertoire is a stock of songs the bird already has, but a bird raised in silence produces nothing usable, so no stock was inherited.
whyWrong.D: A transcript is a fixed, complete record; the text stresses that what is inherited is incomplete and gets filled in by whichever valley the bird grows up in.

tips: Two-sided descriptions like "narrow enough ... and loose enough" point to a word meaning a partly specified pattern.

whyCorrect: The sentences around the underlined one describe the feat: five thousand changes with no row repeating, for about three hours. The underlined sentence adds that the band does all of this from memory, with no music and nobody beating time, and the sentence after it adds that the conductor speaks only calls. Those details are there to show how demanding the feat is, not to define or qualify it.

whyWrong.A: The length of a peal is given in the first sentence, in changes and in hours. The underlined sentence says nothing about how that number is arrived at.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the text is rejected. The passage builds one consistent picture rather than raising and dismissing a claim.
whyWrong.D: No method is named anywhere in the text; the underlined sentence describes how the band works, not which method it rings.

commonMistakes: Treating any sentence full of concrete detail as an example. Ask what job the detail does for the sentences on either side of it.

whyCorrect: Text 1 claims layer counting gives an age good to a few years for the last eleven thousand years. Text 2 does not dispute that; it says counting works only while layers can still be told apart, and that deep in the sheet a year is thinner than the sampling resolution, so ages there come from a flow model with uncertainty of centuries. The author of Text 2 would therefore accept Text 1's accuracy within the countable range and deny that it extends past it.

whyWrong.A: Text 2 never questions the recent ice. Its objection is specifically about the oldest, most compressed part of a core.
whyWrong.B: Text 2 rules this out: the layers there are thinner than the sampling resolution, so more careful counting cannot recover them.
whyWrong.C: Text 2 says the flow model is used where counting fails, not that Text 1's counted ages secretly depend on a model.

tips: When Text 2 limits Text 1 rather than contradicting it, look for the choice that says "only in these conditions" instead of "wrong."

whyCorrect: The text explicitly rejects one explanation and supplies another: "The difference is not craftsmanship but chemistry." Rag needed no acid, while wood pulp is bleached and sized with compounds that leave the sheet acidic from the day it is made. The closing lines make the same point in summary form, that the old sheet is not better made but made of something that does not attack itself.

whyWrong.A: The text links bleaching to acidity and therefore to the loss of strength, so it is wrong to say bleaching left strength unaffected.
whyWrong.C: This is the craftsmanship explanation the text names and rejects in its second sentence.
whyWrong.D: The passage mentions a 1905 newspaper only as an example of acidic paper; it makes no claim about publishers choosing the cheapest stock.

commonMistakes: Picking the choice about skilled old craftsmen because the passage discusses old paper favourably, when the passage denies that craft is the reason.

whyCorrect: This is a detail question, so find the sentence about changing the tune. The text says the barrel is studded with pegs and that "the pegs are shifted by hand when the tune is changed, usually twice a year." Shifting the pegs by hand is the mechanism.

whyWrong.B: The hammers are what strike the bells, but the passage never describes replacing them; only the pegs are moved.
whyWrong.C: The clock turns the barrel and so controls timing, not which notes the pegs call for.
whyWrong.D: The lever disengages the barrel so a carillonneur can play the clavier instead. That silences the barrel; it does not change its tune.

tips: For an "according to the text" question, locate the exact sentence and answer from it, rather than from a general sense of the passage.

whyCorrect: The proposal is a specific causal claim: tower sway feeds back into the ringing, because a leaning tower shortens a bell's swing and returns it to the ringer early. Supporting evidence has to link sway to that early return. Choice D does exactly that, and it does more than correlate, because halving the sway by tying the frame into the masonry removed the effect, which is the closest thing here to a controlled test.

whyWrong.A: A feeling of extra weight is a subjective report about effort, not evidence that the bell comes back early because the tower moved.
whyWrong.B: Comparing brick with stone shows what makes towers sway more. It says nothing about whether the sway changes the timing of the bell.
whyWrong.C: More bells causing more sway again establishes only the cause of sway, leaving the proposed effect on the ringing untested.

commonMistakes: Choosing an option that confirms half the chain. The proposal has two links, sway happening and sway altering the bell's return, and only the second is in doubt.

whyCorrect: Mensah's argument has a precise shape: the reports were assembled from abbreviated shorthand and from memory hours later, so they are not verbatim. Choice D supplies both halves in the reporter's own words, the outlines giving only the drift of a sentence and the printed words being chosen at midnight, four hours after the speech. That is a quotation illustrating the claim rather than merely describing gallery work.

whyWrong.A: Cold and bad light explain physical difficulty, but Mensah's claim is about how shorthand and delayed writing-up alter the words, not about discomfort.
whyWrong.B: This confirms only the relay system, which Mensah mentions in passing. It does not show that the surviving text departs from what was said.
whyWrong.C: The timing of publication says nothing about the accuracy of the words printed.

tips: Match the quotation to the specific mechanism the argument names, not to the general topic.

whyCorrect: To show that acidity rather than age drives the loss of strength, you need a case where the two pull in opposite directions. The 1720 sheet is 150 years older than the 1870 sheet, so age alone predicts it should be weaker, yet its pH is 6.9 against 5.1 and its tear strength is 81 percent against 34 percent, well over double. Age and strength run the wrong way here while acidity and strength still run together, which is exactly the separation the conclusion needs.

whyWrong.A: That the 1560 sheet is the only one above pH 7 is a fact about acidity alone. Since it is also the oldest and strongest, it fits an age explanation just as well.
whyWrong.B: Both post-1800 sheets being below pH 6 groups acidity with recency instead of separating them, so it cannot distinguish the two explanations.
whyWrong.D: The 1935 sheet is both the most acid and the newest, so its weakness is equally consistent with age being the cause.

commonMistakes: Choosing a row that is simply true of the table. A comparison only supports one explanation over another when the two explanations predict different results for it.

whyCorrect: The passage gives one rule and one fact. The rule: a reflection reinforces the direct sound only if it arrives within about fifty milliseconds. The fact: a narrow hall's side walls are close, so their reflections land inside that window. Move the side walls apart and the sound has further to travel, so the reflection arrives later, and past a certain width it falls outside the fifty-millisecond window and is heard as a separate event instead of reinforcement.

whyWrong.A: Further inside the window would require a shorter path, which means narrowing the hall, not widening it.
whyWrong.B: Reverberation decay time is not what the passage is measuring; it discusses when a single early reflection arrives relative to the direct sound.
whyWrong.C: Arrival time depends on distance travelled, so widening the hall must change it. The text says only the length is left untouched.

tips: Turn the physical change into a change in path length first, then ask what that does to arrival time.

whyCorrect: Cleaning does two things here. Removing grime lets more light through, so the window gets brighter. Removing the pitted corrosion removes what had been scattering light across the whole surface, and it is scattering that gives a window its varied, textured look. Take the scattering away and the light passes straight through, so the same window reads as brighter but flatter.

whyWrong.B: Darker contradicts the first sentence of the paragraph, which says grime dims a window; taking the grime off must let more light through.
whyWrong.C: The passage is explicitly about how a window looks from inside, lit from behind, so it cannot be unchanged from that side.
whyWrong.D: Cloudier would follow from adding scattering, but cleaning removes the corrosion layer that was doing the scattering.

commonMistakes: Assuming a cleaned window can only improve. The text separates two effects, and the second one costs the window its texture.

whyCorrect: Both sides are complete sentences: "A datum fixed at one harbour reaches the middle of the country only by levelling from bench mark to bench mark" and "every stage of that chain carries an error of its own." Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma, and "however" is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so it cannot rescue one. The semicolon supplies the required boundary, and the comma after "however" sets it off within the second clause.

whyWrong.B: A comma on each side of "however" leaves two independent clauses spliced together with a comma.
whyWrong.C: This has no punctuation at all before the second clause, producing a run-on, and it also leaves "however" unpunctuated on its left.
whyWrong.D: A colon requires the first clause to introduce or point forward to what follows. Here the second clause qualifies the first rather than delivering something it announced.

tips: Test each side of the blank on its own. Two standalone sentences need a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction.

whyCorrect: "No sparrow had been heard in the valley for a decade after the fire" and "the birds that recolonised it brought the song of the next valley with them" are both complete sentences. The standard way to join two independent clauses with "and" is a comma before the conjunction, which is what this choice gives.

whyWrong.A: A colon introduces an explanation or a list and does not take a coordinating conjunction after it.
whyWrong.C: With no comma, two independent clauses run together on either side of "and"; a comma is required before a coordinating conjunction joining full clauses.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon joins independent clauses on its own. Pairing it with "and" doubles up the join.

commonMistakes: Assuming "and" alone always suffices. It does between two verbs sharing a subject, but not between two complete clauses.

whyCorrect: The comma after "faster" is already printed, so whatever fills the blank has to open a clause that the printed comma closes. That makes it a nonrestrictive relative clause, and nonrestrictive clauses take "which," not "that." Strip it out and the sentence still stands: "The alum-and-rosin size is the reason so many nineteenth-century books can no longer be opened."

whyWrong.A: "That" introduces restrictive clauses, which are never set off by commas, so it clashes with the pair of commas around the clause.
whyWrong.C: Dropping the opening comma leaves an unbalanced pair, with a closing comma after "faster" and nothing matching it.
whyWrong.D: This has the same two faults at once: "that" cannot head a comma-enclosed clause, and the opening comma is missing.

tips: Look for a comma already printed on the far side of the inserted clause; it tells you the clause must be nonrestrictive.

whyCorrect: "When the last row has been rung and the method is complete" is a subordinate clause opening the sentence, and the main clause "the band still has to lower the bells" follows. An introductory subordinate clause is separated from the main clause by a comma.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, "complete the band" runs together and momentarily reads as a noun phrase, leaving the main clause without a boundary.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side, and "When the last row has been rung and the method is complete" cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.C: A colon also needs a complete sentence in front of it, which the introductory "When" clause is not.

commonMistakes: Reaching for a semicolon whenever both halves look long. Check whether the first half can stand alone as a sentence; a clause beginning with "When" cannot.

whyCorrect: The ranges belong to the two hawks, so a possessive is needed, and the possessor is plural. A plural noun already ending in s takes an apostrophe after the s: two hawks' ranges.

whyWrong.A: "Hawks's" adds a second s to a plural that already ends in s; that form is used for singular nouns ending in s, not plurals.
whyWrong.C: The plain plural "hawks" shows no possession, leaving two nouns stacked with no relationship marked.
whyWrong.D: "Hawk's" is singular possessive, which contradicts "two" and would mean the ranges belong to one bird.

tips: Decide the number of the owner first, then place the apostrophe: hawk's for one, hawks' for more than one.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets a past reference point, 1904, and describes a state that was already in place before it and had lasted two generations. A past action or state completed before another past moment takes the past perfect: had been.

whyWrong.A: "Has been" is present perfect and measures duration up to now, which clashes with a sentence anchored in 1904.
whyWrong.B: Simple past "was" states the situation in 1904 but loses the sense that the two generations ran up to that year rather than after it.
whyWrong.C: "Would be" points forward from a past moment, making the tuning standard only after 1904, the reverse of what "for two generations" before the rebuild says.

tips: "By the time" plus a past event is a reliable signal for the past perfect in the other clause.

whyCorrect: Find the subject by stripping the prepositional phrases: the subject is "the proportion," not "tin" or "the alloy," because a noun inside "of tin" or "in the alloy" cannot be the subject. "Proportion" is singular, so the present-tense verb takes the singular form, ranges.

whyWrong.A: "Are ranging" is plural and also puts a permanent, unchanging fact into a progressive tense.
whyWrong.B: "Ranging" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the sentence would be left with no main verb.
whyWrong.D: "Range" agrees with a plural subject, which is what you get by wrongly taking "tin" or "bells" as the subject.

commonMistakes: Letting the nearest noun before the verb set the agreement. Cross out every "of" and "in" phrase before you choose.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states a problem: a pipe voiced to speak promptly in the workshop turns harsh in a stone church. The second states what the voicer does about it, softening the attacks after installation. The second is the response to the first, so the transition has to mark cause and effect.

whyWrong.A: "Nonetheless" signals that the second sentence holds despite the first, but here it follows from the first.
whyWrong.B: "In addition" would make the two sentences parallel items in a list, when the second is a consequence of the first.
whyWrong.D: "By contrast" sets the sentences against each other, yet they agree: the workshop setting misleads, so the voicer corrects for it.

tips: Ask whether the second sentence is a new point, an opposing point, or a result. Only one of those needs a contrast word.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says what a conservator does not do and why tape is unacceptable. The second describes the method actually used, tissue and reversible starch paste. The second replaces the first, so the transition has to signal substitution.

whyWrong.A: "Therefore" claims the tissue method follows logically from the faults of tape; the relationship is one of alternative, not deduction.
whyWrong.B: "Likewise" says the two are similar, but the passage sets them in opposition: one is irreversible and one is reversible.
whyWrong.C: "In fact" intensifies or corrects the previous statement, whereas this sentence changes the subject to a different technique.

commonMistakes: Reading any "X is bad, Y is good" pair as cause and effect. A rejected option followed by the adopted one calls for a replacement transition.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says the note can be calculated in advance and the arithmetic is easy. The second says the calculation does not survive the pour, because uneven shrinkage leaves the casting off the intended note. The second undercuts the first, so the transition must be concessive.

whyWrong.A: "Therefore" would make the failure of the calculation a consequence of the calculation being easy, which is not what the text says.
whyWrong.B: "Similarly" claims the two sentences make the same kind of point; the second denies what the first grants.
whyWrong.C: "For instance" introduces an example of the previous claim, but a casting that misses the intended note is a counterexample to it.

tips: When the second sentence contains a negative like "no calculation survives," check whether it is cancelling the sentence before it.

whyCorrect: The goal is a difficulty peculiar to the instrument, so the sentence has to name a problem and show why it is a problem for the player. Only this choice combines the last three notes: the wires stretch, so a heavy bell sounds late, so the player has to strike early by an amount that differs bell by bell. That is the difficulty, stated with its cause and its consequence for playing.

whyWrong.B: The number of bells and how they are hung is background information; nothing here is difficult for a player.
whyWrong.C: Describing the linkage from clavier to clapper explains how the instrument works but names no difficulty at all.
whyWrong.D: The length of the wires is only one ingredient. On its own it is a fact about tall towers, not a problem the player has to solve.

tips: For a stated goal like "explain a difficulty," check that the sentence actually contains a difficulty, not just a true detail from the notes.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain why change ringing developed in England rather than elsewhere, so the sentence needs the English practice, the capability it creates, and the contrast with elsewhere. Only this choice has all three: full-circle hanging leaves the bell mouth upward, the ringer can hold it and so alter the order, and the small arc used elsewhere does not allow it.

whyWrong.A: This gives the resting position but not what a ringer does with it, and it never mentions practice outside England, so it cannot explain a difference.
whyWrong.C: How English bells are hung is only the first step; without the ability to hold a bell and change the order, it explains nothing about change ringing.
whyWrong.D: Describing the smaller arc used elsewhere supplies one side of the comparison and leaves out both the English method and its consequence.

commonMistakes: Choosing a single accurate note. A "why X rather than Y" goal always needs both sides plus the mechanism connecting them.

whyCorrect: The goal is narrow: why the mould is buried in sand. The answer has to pair the burying with its purpose, and this choice does, linking the packed sand to the outward pressure of several tonnes of molten metal and to the burst mould and ruined casting that would otherwise follow.

whyWrong.B: How the core is built and dried belongs to an earlier stage and says nothing about the sand.
whyWrong.C: Sweeping the cope to a profile is about shaping the mould, not about what protects it during the pour.
whyWrong.D: This names the consequence of failure but never mentions sand, so it does not explain why the mould is buried.

tips: When the goal names one specific thing, the correct sentence usually mentions that thing and a reason in the same breath.

whyCorrect: The passage is explicit that the marking pass cuts nothing free; the deeper blade and the saw do that. What it does instead is fix the size of every block hours in advance so that a hundred men produce identical rectangles. Laying out dimensions before any cutting happens is planning, so the pass was less a cut than a plan.

whyWrong.B: Nothing in the text describes danger. The grid removes uncertainty rather than creating it.
whyWrong.C: A delay would mean time wasted, but the marking pass does necessary work that makes the later cuts uniform.
whyWrong.D: A flourish is decorative and inessential, and the grid is what keeps a hundred men producing the same block.

commonMistakes: Missing the "less a cut than" frame, which tells you the blank must name something other than cutting.

whyCorrect: The passage defines water activity as how much water is free to take part in a reaction rather than bound to sugar, salt or protein. It then says honey and a fig can hold similar amounts of water yet behave differently because in honey almost none of it is available. "Available" is therefore standing in for that definition: free to react.

whyWrong.A: Drinkability is never discussed. The passage is about whether water can participate chemically, not about who might drink it.
whyWrong.C: Visibility is irrelevant; the bound and free water in honey look exactly the same.
whyWrong.D: Ease of removal is a different property. Water in honey is bound to sugar, but the question is what it can do, not how hard it is to drive off.

tips: When a passage supplies a definition, the tested word almost always echoes that definition rather than its dictionary meaning.

whyCorrect: The passage twice sets up the same structure: the action does not merely do the obvious housekeeping job, it also shapes the cheese. Brushing redistributes organisms and presses them into the paste so the rind thickens evenly; turning moves moisture back through the body. Each gesture is helping to form what the cheese becomes, which is what formative means, and it is the point the opening sentence promised when it said the round only looks like housekeeping.

whyWrong.B: Ceremonial means performed for form's sake without practical effect, the opposite of what the two examples establish.
whyWrong.C: Speed is never mentioned; the passage is about what the gestures accomplish, not how quickly they are done.
whyWrong.D: Optional contradicts the whole argument, since without brushing the rind thickens in patches and without turning the moisture stays at the underside.

commonMistakes: Reading "looks like housekeeping" as the claim rather than as the idea the passage immediately denies.

whyCorrect: Cold storage cures sprouting but causes sugaring; warm storage cures sugaring but causes sprouting. The growers' method uses cold storage for the whole season and then a two-week warming that reverses the sugar without waking the eyes, so each fault is dealt with by its own measure at its own time. Treating them that way means treating them as separable, and the sentence contrasts this with a single problem fixed by a single setting.

whyWrong.A: Trivial would mean the faults hardly matter, yet growers reorganise their whole storage routine around them.
whyWrong.C: Identical is what the sentence explicitly rejects, since it contrasts the growers' view with treating them as one problem.
whyWrong.D: Unavoidable contradicts the passage, which describes a practice that avoids both faults.

tips: The words after "rather than" tell you what the blank must oppose; here it must oppose "a single problem with a single setting."

whyCorrect: The passage describes a staircase of ponds, water moving from the largest to the smallest, growing heavier at every step until the last pan throws down crystals. The colon then explains the blank directly: each pond does one part of a concentration no single pond could manage. A design built as an ordered series of stages is sequential.

whyWrong.A: Symbolic would mean the arrangement stands for something; the passage gives it a strictly practical job.
whyWrong.B: Improvised suggests no plan, but the ponds are graded in a deliberate order of decreasing size.
whyWrong.D: Wasteful conflicts with a design in which every pond performs a necessary part of the work.

tips: When a colon follows the blank, the clause after it is a definition of the missing word.

whyCorrect: The text spends its first two sentences on the mechanism, fissures that let air move down in summer and reverse in winter, and its last sentence on the outcome, a chamber never sealed and never dry whose humidity the cheesemakers could not reproduce above ground. Purpose questions ask what the whole text is doing, and this one explains a natural ventilation system and notes that it resisted imitation.

whyWrong.B: The fissures are mentioned as air paths, and the text never says how they were formed.
whyWrong.C: No comparison of the resulting cheese is offered. The difficulty described is technical, not a claim about quality.
whyWrong.D: Both seasons are described as producing airflow, in opposite directions, and productivity is never raised.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice about a detail the text mentions once instead of the idea both halves of the text build toward.

whyCorrect: Read the sentence in position. Before it, the text describes fragments being jostled until each wears a raised white rim. The underlined sentence gives the state that produces, a field of pale discs packed edge to edge. After it, the text says the rims stay visible in the finished sheet as a record of how it formed. So the underlined sentence supplies the middle stage whose rims the final sentence then interprets as evidence of the ice's history.

whyWrong.A: The text says the opposite: ice does form in rough water, just in discs rather than a sheet at first.
whyWrong.B: No calm-water ice is described anywhere for comparison; calm is mentioned only as the condition under which the discs freeze together.
whyWrong.D: The size is included as description, and the passage never uses it to distinguish this ice from other kinds.

tips: For a function question, read the sentence before and the sentence after; the answer is usually the relationship between them.

whyCorrect: The opening sentence states the thesis, that a curing season is imposed rather than chosen, and everything after it supports that. The fish are present for only weeks, their fat content changes across the run and with it how they salt and keep, and the curers followed the shoals down the coast on the fish's calendar. So both when the season happened and what the pack was like were set by the herring.

whyWrong.A: The text contrasts early and late barrels but never says which curers preferred; it says the fish's condition set what they got.
whyWrong.B: The causal arrow runs the other way. Fat content determines how much salt the fish take up, not the reverse.
whyWrong.C: Following the shoals extended the season through the summer, not indefinitely, and the passage frames it as being led by the fish rather than as a way to gain time.

commonMistakes: Choosing a detail from the middle of the passage. The main idea is usually the claim the details are assembled to support.

whyCorrect: The passage names the survival mechanism explicitly: what keeps the frog alive is that the ice stays outside the cells, and the liver floods the blood with glucose that enters the cells and holds water in them so they do not collapse. That is a chemical change protecting the cells while ice forms around them, which is what this choice says.

whyWrong.A: The two thirds figure describes what happens, not a requirement for survival; the passage never says that fraction must freeze.
whyWrong.B: The text states the heart stops and there is no measurable respiration.
whyWrong.D: The frog does freeze. The glucose does not prevent freezing; it keeps the ice outside the cells.

tips: When a passage contains a sentence beginning "What keeps it alive is," that sentence is the main idea in miniature.
